title: London cop's jail sentence a sign of changing times: Indigenous grand chief
subtitle: The head of an Indigenous umbrella group says the 12-month jail sentence for a London police officer convicted in an Indigenous woman's custody death would have been an unlikely outcome years ago.
article: The head of a First Nations umbrella group says the 12-month jail sentence for a London police officer convicted in an Indigenous woman's custody death would have been an unlikely outcome years ago.

Const. Nicholas Doering, 30, was sentenced Monday after being convicted last November of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life in the Sept. 7, 2016, death of Debra Chrisjohn.
"I think, for sure, it's a product of its times," Joel Abram, Grand Chief of the Association of Iroquois and Allied Indians, said of the sentencing.

Abram, whose organization represents First Nations including several in Southwestern Ontario, was one of nearly 250 people who watched Justice Renee Pomerance deliver her sentence over a video broadcast on YouTube.
The Crown sought a sentence of 20 to 30 months, while the defence pushed for probation and community service as part of a conditional sentence.

Abrams credits an increased awareness of the plight of Canada's Indigenous people, including the fallout from residential schools, the Sixties Scoop and the inquiry into missing and murdered Indigenous females for making the mistreatment harder to ignore.
"It would have been swept under the rug . . . in the past," he said of the death of an Indigenous woman in police custody.
But there's still a long way to go, Abram said, calling increased police accountability a key part of building trust with marginalized communities.
"I'd like to see some other follow-up actions including his employment being formally terminated," he said of Doering, who was suspended from the force Monday.

London police Chief Steve Williams said Doering, who is appealing his case, is suspended with pay - police chiefs in Ontario don't have authority to withhold salaries from suspended officers - while the appeal works its way through the courts.

Doering arrested Chrisjohn, 39, after she was found trying to get into vehicles in east London while high on crystal meth. He transferred her into OPP custody on an outstanding warrant, falsely telling two officers that she'd been medically cleared, court heard.

Paramedics were called to the Elgin OPP detachment, where they found a motionless Chrisjohn lying on the floor of her cell, breathing irregularly. She died at the hospital from cardiac arrest connected to crystal meth use, the court heard.
Doering, who was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, has twice apologized publicly to Chrisjohn's family, but they have dismissed his words as insincere.

Abram, an Oneida member, said he's hopeful the jail sentence will begin to bring closure to the family of Chrisjohn, a mother of 11 from the Oneida of the Thames First Nation, an Indigenous community southwest of London.
"I think that would give a lot hope to the family and let them begin the healing," he said.
